## Slide 2 · Goals for today

Four goals today. We learn about the use of R packages. We understand the main
object types in R and their practical relevance. We learn how to transform
object types into each other. And we hear about some useful helper functions and
about the concept of vectorisation.

This is the last session of the general introduction — after this we turn to
working with real data.

## Slide 4 · R packages

One cool thing about R is that there is a great community of R users that write
objects and functions which perform useful purposes, and make them available to
all. This process of making objects available to others is done via R packages.

You can think of an R package as a collection of assignments and documentations
that people pass around.

If you install R, you can use all objects that you defined for yourself and all
objects that are pre-defined in R. If you want to use objects defined by someone
else in their package, you need to install this package first.

## Slide 5 · Installing packages

The official way to distribute packages is via CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive
Network. To install a package that was deployed on CRAN you execute
`install.packages()` with the name of the package as a string.

To install the package `ineq`, for instance, you write `install.packages("ineq")`.

For packages that were not yet released on CRAN — for example development
versions on GitHub — other functions are available; the tutorials cover that.

Note that installing happens once per machine, not once per script.

## Slide 6 · Calling objects defined in packages

One object defined in `ineq` is the function `Gini()`, which computes the Gini
coefficient. Simply calling `Gini()` does not work — R does not know where to
look for it.

You need to tell R that `Gini()` is defined by the package `ineq`, and you do
that with the double colon. You may think of `::` as building a bridge between
your R session and all objects defined in a package.

A sometimes more convenient way is to use `library()` at the beginning of your
script. This attaches the package and makes available all objects of `ineq` in
your current R session, so you can then write `Gini()` directly.

## Slide 7 · Packages and masking

Packages are written by many different people, so it is not unlikely that two
packages assign the same name to different objects. If you then attach both
packages, the assignment of the earlier package will be masked by the later one.

You can try this by attaching the two packages `dplyr` and `plm`. In such cases
you must use the double colon to access the masked object of the first package.

As a general rule: always use `::` whenever masking is a potential problem. It
makes your code much easier to understand for you and for others, because the
reader can see immediately where a function comes from. The function
`conflicts()` shows you all names for which conflicts currently exist.

## Slide 8 · Recap questions

Six recap questions. Work through them in pairs — they are exactly the kind of
conceptual question that separates "I can copy the code" from "I understand what
the code does".

The fourth one is the one worth spending time on: `::` is explicit and local but
verbose; `library()` is convenient but changes the meaning of every later name in
the script.

## Slide 10 · Why types matter

Back to the Chambers quote from session two, but this time we focus on the first
half. We have learned quite a bit about functions; now we turn to objects.

We must distinguish different object types because functions operate differently
depending on the type of object we are processing. Adding up numbers is
something different from adding up words — and R has to know which of the two
you mean.

Fortunately, there are only a few basic types you must know about; more complex
types are natural modifications of these. The most general type of object in R
is a vector.

## Slide 11 · The basic type hierarchy

This is the map for the rest of the session, and it is worth memorising.

At the very top sit objects. They split into vectors and NULL. Vectors split
into atomic vectors and lists, which are sometimes called generic vectors.

Atomic vectors come in four types that matter for us: logical, integer, double
and character.

Today we deal with atomic vectors first, in dark blue, and then with lists, in
red. Among the more specific vector types we will meet factors and data frames
next time — and both of them are built on top of what we do today.

## Slide 12 · Atomic vectors

Atomic vectors are composed only of objects of the same type. We say that an
atomic vector is of the same type as its elements, and we can test for this type
using the function `typeof()`.

Four main types matter. Logical: only two options, TRUE or FALSE, often the
result of logical operations such as four greater than two. Integer: a whole
number followed by a capital L, often the result of counting. Double: a number
with a decimal sign — this is the standard number you will use throughout.
Character: might contain all kinds of tokens and starts and ends with quotation
marks.

Note the trap in the last column: `"2"` in quotation marks is a character, not a
number. You cannot do arithmetic with it, and that is a very common source of
confusion later when data is imported.

## Slide 13 · Creating atomic vectors

The easiest way to create atomic vectors is the function `c()`, which stands for
concatenate.

The number of elements that are part of a vector is its length, and you can test
for the length of a vector using `length()`.

And `c()` can also be used to merge atomic vectors of arbitrary length — note
that this gives you one flat vector of length six, not a nested structure. That
is a genuine difference to lists, which we come to later.

## Slide 14 · Coercion

Sometimes we might want to change the type of an atomic vector. In this context
the functions starting with `as.` and `is.` are useful: substitute the star for
the type of vector, and you can test and transform them.

Here we start with the character `"2"`, check that it is not a double, transform
it into a double, and check again.

But beware of some counter-intuitive transformation behaviour. What does
`as.integer(22.9)` return? It returns 22 — it truncates rather than rounds. And
`as.logical(99)` returns TRUE, because in R every non-zero number counts as
TRUE. Try both before you assume.

## Slide 15 · Intermediate exercises

Four exercises. The second one already contains a surprise: although three of
the four numbers are whole numbers, the vector is of type double, because 2.4
forces all of them to be doubles.

The fourth question is the important one and anticipates the next concept: you
*can* create that vector, but R will silently coerce everything to character,
because character is the only type that can hold all of them. Check with
`typeof()`.

## Slide 17 · Sequences: `seq()`

There are some types of atomic vectors that you create frequently: sequences of
numbers, concatenated words, or repetitions.

For sequences you use `seq()`. `from` and `to` are the starting and end values.
`by` gives the increment steps and must be numeric. `length.out` gives the
desired length of the final sequence. And `along.with` creates a sequence of the
same length as another object — which is very useful for index vectors.

Note that only one of the last three can be used at a time: you either specify
the step size or the length, not both, because together they would over-determine
the sequence.

## Slide 18 · Pasting and repeating

For case two, concatenated words, you may use the function `paste()` with the
argument `sep`, which says how the input vectors should be separated.

This is useful, for instance, if you want to create file names: pasting
`"file_"`, the sequence one to four and `".pdf"` with an empty separator gives
you four file names in one line. Note how `paste()` is vectorised here — one call
produces four strings, because `seq(1,4)` has four elements.

And finally, if you want to repeat something, use `rep()`.

## Slide 19 · Indexing

Indexing means referencing a particular position of a vector. You do this by
adding the position in square brackets to the end of the vector name. So
`v_c[3]` returns the third element of the vector `v_c`.

You can also use this logic to replace elements: assigning to `v_c[3]` overwrites
the third element.

Now try the last line yourself and watch what actually happens when you assign to
a position beyond the current length. Discuss in pairs whether the result is what
you expected — and what would happen if you assigned to position ten instead.

## Slide 20 · Vectorisation

One reason why atomic vectors are so popular is that they allow for very fast
computations. For the computer it is much easier to work with sets of objects
that all behave the same way — which is exactly what "all elements have the same
type" buys us.

Vectorisation means that an operation is applied to each element of a vector.
Squaring `v_2` squares every element, without you writing any loop.

To vectorise a task means to write it in a way that operations are applied to
atomic vectors. In R you should do that whenever possible. The slower
alternative are loops, which we learn about later and which are unavoidable in
certain situations.

## Slide 21 · Intermediate exercises

Four exercises again.

For the index vector, `seq(along.with = ...)` from two slides ago is the elegant
route.

The third one contains the pedagogical point: the log of a negative number is
not defined, so R returns NaN and issues a warning — but it does not stop. Your
vector now silently contains NaNs. That is exactly the kind of thing you must
learn to notice.

The fourth question asks you to discover the coercion hierarchy yourself:
logical becomes integer becomes double becomes character. R always coerces to
the most general type present.

## Slide 23 · Lists

Lists are the second major type of vectors, sometimes called generic vectors.

The difference to atomic vectors is that lists may contain objects of different
types — here a numeric vector, a character vector and a logical vector, all in
one object. The type of a list is therefore always just "list".

Lists can become complex quickly, so use `str()` to get an overview. Read the
output carefully: "List of 3" is the number of list elements. The abbreviations
num, chr and logi are the types of the elements. The bracket expressions are the
lengths of the individual elements. And the rest is a preview of the content.

Note that the three elements have different lengths — two, two and three. That
is perfectly fine for a list and impossible for an atomic vector.

## Slide 24 · Naming and indexing of lists

The different elements of lists can be named, which makes them far more readable
than position numbers.

You can retrieve the names using `names()`. You can subset the list using the
names with single square brackets — and this gives you back a list containing
that one element. And you can access the elements of the sublists with double
square brackets, which gives you the content itself, here a character vector.

That distinction between single and double brackets is the single most confusing
thing about lists for beginners, so test both and compare the results with
`typeof()`.

Alternatively, use the dollar shortcut, which does the same as double brackets.

## Slide 25 · Practical differences to atomic vectors

There are two very important practical differences to atomic vectors:
vectorisation does not work for lists, and indexing works differently.

To illustrate the first: multiplying an atomic vector by two works elementwise,
multiplying a list by two throws an error. The list does not guarantee that its
elements are numbers, so R refuses.

To illustrate the second, compare the two `typeof()` calls: single brackets give
you a list, double brackets give you the double inside it.

Lists are fundamental to more complex data structures we will encounter later —
in particular data frames, which are nothing but lists of equally long vectors.

## Slide 26 · `NA` — absent elements

There are two "strange" data types worth knowing: `NA` and `NULL`.

`NA` is used to represent absent elements of vectors. This happens frequently
when vectors contain observations — no real data set is complete.

Many functions behave differently when NAs are present; remember the `na.rm`
argument from session two.

You test for NA using `is.na()`, which returns a logical vector of the same
length. To check whether a vector contains any missing values at all, use
`anyNA()`, which returns one TRUE or FALSE.

## Slide 27 · `NULL` — the absent vector

`NULL` is in fact a data type in itself, but in practice it is best thought of as
a vector of length zero. Calling `c()` without arguments returns NULL, its length
is zero, and `is.null()` tests for it.

You might use NULL mainly in two instances: to represent an empty vector of
arbitrary type, and to represent an absent vector.

Keep the distinction from NA clear: NA is an absent element inside a vector, NULL
is an absent vector. A vector of three NAs has length three; NULL has length
zero.

## Slide 28 · Intermediate exercises

Create a list with three named elements.

Element A asks for the square root of numbers from minus two to eight — and
again the negative values will produce NaN with a warning. That is intentional:
you should see it a second time and recognise it immediately.

Element B combines `seq()` with step size and `log()`.

Element C combines the pre-defined vector `letters` with `paste()` and a
sequence, producing a1, b2, c3 and so on up to g7.

## Slide 29 · Wrap up

To wrap up the object types: remember the hierarchy — objects split into vectors
and NULL, vectors split into atomic vectors and lists, and atomic vectors come in
four flavours.

The central take-aways concern three practical abilities: how to test for and
transform these types, how to index them, and how to create typical instances.

Beyond that we learned about vectorisation and why it is so attractive in R, and
we encountered the strange types NA, NULL, and NaN — the last one turning up
whenever a numerical operation is undefined.

## Slide 30 · Summary and outlook

Next time we will learn about two more advanced object types: factors and data
frames. And we will see how our knowledge about the basic object types helps us
to deal with the more advanced ones, and how they relate to each other — a data
frame, as mentioned, is a list of equally long vectors.

The usual three tasks until next session: the feedback survey, the tutorials, and
the exercises with discussion in the Moodle forum.
